dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract

evidence.note: Systematic source read of every major reference file (app.rb, models, db, markdown_renderer, liquid_setup, all migrations, all middleware, jobs/helpers/seed, all liquid views, spec helper + env vars) before writing Rust.
Dug into rack-protection gem internals (XSS/frame protection, html? definition, default protections) to recover the exact header/CSP contract rather than trusting a surface read.
Wrote and later revised durable behavioral notes (MEMORY.md, rj-port.md) — a persistent reference model, not front-loaded scratch work.
Inspected Sequel migration bookkeeping + full DDL and empirically probed RedCarpet/Rouge output quirks (block joins, lang map, inline edge cases) to capture rendering edge behavior.
Ran the reference live and captured JSON/HTML/feed/etag/validation responses across register/me/post/comment/tags/search/media/feeds and header sets — empirical confirmation, not code-only.
Empirically recovered job-queue claim semantics: cross-runtime processing, runner failure injection, dead-letter timing and dead_letter_reason compared against the reference.
Kept revisiting the reference late in the horizon as new mismatches surfaced (404/410 behavior, audit.log format, feed diffs, frozen-time), showing sustained orientation.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent read all major reference source AND ran the reference live to empirically confirm behavior, even reading gem internals to nail header contracts, and built durable notes (MEMORY.md/rj-port.md) it later revised. It captured edge cases across every subsystem (soft-delete/validation, CSP, pagination, markdown quirks, BEGIN IMMEDIATE/dead-letter claim semantics) and kept returning to the reference to resolve ambiguities throughout the whole trajectory rather than front-loading — matching the level-10 anchor's durable, dual-sourced, self-correcting model sustained across the horizon.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Extensive reference reconnaissance before decomposing; understanding-first posture that feeds a subsystem breakdown.
Built golden corpus, trace surveys, and per-route header sets as parity done-checks, then wrote the plan/notes to MEMORY.md and rj-port.md — plan is written down before coding.

Six explicit dependency-aware milestones: DB/migrations first (foundational for shared jobs schema), markdown labeled 'Hardest parity target' (risk tiering), server/routing/middleware, routes/models/search, HTML views, and cross-runtime job queue (BEGIN IMMEDIATE/retry/dead-letter) as its own milestone.
TaskUpdate status transitions track each milestone's state (in_progress/completed) across the long horizon — sustained milestone tracking, not just an opening plan.

Cross-runtime job-queue milestone verified with a dedicated cross-runtime processing/dead-letter test — concrete exit check, but this hardest shared-state interface was sequenced late rather than first.
Revised rj-port.md as discovered complexity emerged, showing some plan revision (though light rather than continuous reshaping).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent produced an explicit, dependency-aware milestone breakdown (steps 90-95) with a sensible order (schema/foundations before feeds/views), each milestone paired with a concrete parity check (golden markdown harness, differential comparison, cross-runtime job test, trace replay), and the plan was written to memory files and referenced/updated throughout — squarely matching anchor 8. It exhibits risk tiering (markdown flagged 'hardest') but falls short of 10 because the most cross-runtime-coupled interface (job-queue claim semantics) was tackled as a late milestone rather than de-risked first, and mid-course re-planning was minimal.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification

evidence.note: Generates a golden corpus from the reference — building an oracle rather than eyeballing.
Runs the reference server side-by-side and captures JSON/HTML for register/me/post/comment/tags/search/feeds/etag, the raw material for differential comparison.
Writes reusable comparison scripts (cmp.py, run_cmp.py) that diff both servers' responses — a genuine reusable harness, not manual curls.
replay.py replays 500 golden HTTP traces against the live service, a large automated regression corpus.
Cross-runtime job queue exercised against the real reference on a shared DB, including write-contention/claim races — the hardest interop element.
Rate-limit header comparison, ETag/conditional GET, byte-exact media upload test, concurrency smoke test — matching the grader's specialized checks.
Health latency ratio measured and no-Ruby/binary-size hard-constraint verification wired into the checks.
Differential suite re-run repeatedly after fixes and under frozen time — used as a continuous regression gate across the long horizon.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent built multiple reusable differential harnesses (cmp.py, replay.py, navcmp.py) that compare its Rust service against a live reference across nearly every subsystem — routing, JSON/HTML (structural tag-tree comparison), feeds, ETag/conditional GET, rate-limit headers, byte-exact media, concurrency, and the shared-DB cross-runtime job queue including claim races — plus hard-constraint checks (no-Ruby, binary size, health latency) and re-ran the suite as a regression gate under frozen time. This clearly exceeds the level-8 anchor and spans essentially the full level-10 list. I place it at 9 rather than 10 only because the file shows tool-call headers, not script internals, so I cannot fully confirm the normalization faithfully mirrors the grader's recursive dynamic-key elision and UUID rules.

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking

evidence.note: Created an explicit 6-subsystem task ledger (TaskCreate) covering db/migrations, markdown, server/middleware, routes+models, views, job queue — a structured done-vs-remaining checklist.
TaskUpdate status transitions (in_progress/completed) tracked as each subsystem passed, keeping a running picture of coverage across the long horizon.
Built a reusable differential comparison harness and re-ran it across many subsystems/flows, giving harness-backed pass/fail signal rather than recollection.

After a deadlock forced a db-pool change (shared code), explicitly re-ran the navbar comparison and the full differential suite — checking that a fix to shared code didn't regress previously-passing areas.
Re-ran the 500-trace golden replay at multiple milestones (post-404 fixes, post-pool-fix, final frozen-time), using broad coverage checks to confirm state rather than trusting the last edit.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained a subsystem task ledger and updated it as pieces passed, backed it with a reusable differential harness re-run across subsystems, and after a shared-code (db pool) change it re-ran both a targeted comparison and the full suite to guard against regression — squarely matching the level-8 behaviors of per-subsystem tracking and regression detection. It falls short of 10 because the ledger is coarse (binary in_progress/completed over 6 tasks, no explicit passing/failing/not-yet-attempted distinction) and the action-only log shows no explicit 'stuck → change tactic' reallocation reasoning, so I place it at 7.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence

evidence.note: Stress test surfaced a deadlock/hang; agent diagnosed root cause and redesigned the DB connection model (introduced a pool in db.rs), then re-stress-tested, ran cross-runtime write-contention, and re-ran the full differential suite — a design-level change with whole-subsystem re-verification.

Instead of patching one diff, returned to the reference to derive true 404/410 halt behavior across API/HTML/media routes, changed API 404s to JSON, edited multiple files, then re-ran golden trace replay to confirm the class of failures closed.
Cross-runtime job test + failure injection led to re-deriving dead-letter timing and dead_letter_reason from the reference and correcting jobs.rs, then rebuilding to verify parity.
Iterative markdown correction against a golden corpus, and proactively generated edge-case (161) and 300-case fuzz (172) corpora from the reference to catch divergences before fixing them.
Wrote and later updated a behavioral-model/memory file (after the pool fix), showing the model/plan was revised as assumptions were falsified.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent repeatedly treats mismatches as signals to revisit design rather than papering over them: the deadlock-driven redesign of the DB connection model (pool) with a full differential re-run, and the reference-derived correction of the whole 404/410 response class with golden-replay re-verification, are textbook level-8 behavior (revisit design, re-verify the affected subsystem). It also re-derives job-queue dead-letter semantics from the reference and updates its behavioral-model memory. It stops short of level 10 because there is no decisive mid-course library/model swap when a crate can't reach parity (markdown/HTML were hand-built from the outset), and the evidence is an action log without visible reasoning, so I anchor at a strong 8.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring

evidence.note: Early size-awareness (measures reference sizes, checks spec sizes) and probes a heavy crate stack build for FTS5 — screening for the 40MB/crate constraints before committing.

Treats shared-DB claim semantics as a matched live contract: frames the queue as BEGIN IMMEDIATE/retry-backoff/dead-letter, then runs cross-runtime job processing, dead-letter injection vs reference timing, dead_letter_reason comparison, and a write-contention test — the deepest, most iterative constraint guarding.
Explicitly compares /_health latency between the Rust service and reference — actively monitors the latency-parity gate.

Verifies binary size + no-Ruby constraints, data-dir layout, and confirms no rust/ruby process via ps -C — process-tree/no-embed audit, but done as near-end verification rather than a continuously re-run gate.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent actively guards every hard constraint: it screens crate/size early, explicitly measures the /_health latency ratio, audits binary size and process tree for no-Ruby, and — most notably — treats the shared-DB BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter semantics as a matched contract tested repeatedly against the live reference. This squarely matches the level-8 anchor. It stops short of 10 because the size/no-Ruby/process-tree audits read as late-stage verification passes rather than standing gates re-run on every build to catch a violation the instant it is introduced; only the shared-DB interop reached that iterative standard.

rubric.task_read: A very long-horizon, high-complexity reverse-engineering-and-reimplementation task: port a broad Sinatra blog app to Rust with structural parity across ~two dozen subsystems (routing, ORM semantics, auth, CSRF/sessions, rate limiting, feeds, Markdown, FTS5 search, media, caching headers, a cross-runtime SQLite job queue, admin/audit). The reference app IS the spec, so success hinges on disciplined probing of reference behavior, subsystem decomposition, and a differential-testing loop that compares against the live reference. Hard constraints (no Ruby runtime/bridge crates, 40 MB binary, latency parity, exact shared-DB claim semantics) add ongoing compliance pressure. This is near the ceiling of meta-work demand: deep upfront orientation, milestone structure, and self-correcting verification are decisive.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract
dimensions.description: Systematically reading/probing the Ruby reference to recover exact behavior (routes, ORM query shapes, header contracts, job-queue claim semantics, env vars) before and while porting.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The reference is the only spec; guessing behavior for CSRF, rate-limit windows, ETag/cache-control, RFC 5988 links, or BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics leads to silent parity failures that are expensive to find later.

anchors.0: Starts writing Rust from assumptions about 'a typical blog' without reading the reference source or running it.
anchors.3: Skims a few route files; grasps the happy path but never inspects headers, ORM ordering/soft-delete, env-var handling, or the jobs table schema.
anchors.5: Reads the major reference files and enumerates routes/models/templates; probes a handful of endpoints to confirm status/headers; identifies the RJ_* vars and the shared jobs schema.
anchors.8: Methodically maps each subsystem to its reference behavior, capturing edge cases (soft-delete, eager loading, validation errors, CSP contents, pagination link format) and empirically confirming responses by curling the running reference rather than trusting the code read.
anchors.10: Builds a durable behavioral reference model (notes/tables of every contract header, dynamic-key set, ORM ordering, retry/backoff and dead-letter rules, claim transaction) derived from BOTH source and live probing, and keeps revisiting the reference to resolve ambiguities as new mismatches surface — orientation sustained across the whole horizon, not front-loaded.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the port into ordered, independently verifiable subsystems (skeleton/health → routing → ORM → templates → auth/CSRF → feeds → search → media → job queue → admin/audit) each with a done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With ~two dozen interdependent subsystems under a hard binary/latency budget, an undifferentiated push loses the plot; correct ordering (e.g. DB schema and health before feeds) prevents rework and lets parity be measured incrementally.

anchors.0: One monolithic effort with no sub-goals; jumps between unrelated features reactively.
anchors.3: A vague mental list ('do routes, then auth'); milestones have no explicit completion criteria.
anchors.5: Explicit subsystem breakdown with a sensible order and a rough done-signal per piece (e.g. 'posts CRUD returns matching JSON').
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan where each milestone has a concrete parity check and risky/foundational pieces (shared jobs schema, session/CSRF, header contracts) are sequenced early; plan is written down and referenced.
anchors.10: Milestone structure that tiers work by parity risk and cross-runtime coupling, defines a crisp exit test per milestone, sequences to de-risk the hardest shared-state interfaces first, and is revised as discovered complexity reshapes the remaining plan.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately building a way to compare the Rust service against the reference on the same requests (status, normalized headers, structure-eliding JSON/HTML/feed comparison, byte-exact uploads, job-queue interop).
dimensions.why_it_matters: Grading is structural diff against the reference; without an own differential harness that mirrors the grader's normalization rules, the agent is flying blind and cannot know which of two dozen subsystems actually match.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'it compiles' / manual eyeballing of one endpoint.
anchors.3: Runs a few curls by hand and compares output visually; no normalization, no reuse.
anchors.5: Scripts side-by-side requests to both servers for the main endpoints and diffs responses, catching obvious status/body mismatches.
anchors.8: Builds a reusable differential harness that normalizes the way the grader does (elides dynamic JSON keys, collapses HTML whitespace, treats headers as a set, normalizes UUID/timestamps), covers most subsystems, and exercises the cross-runtime job queue against the real reference.
anchors.10: A comprehensive, automated parity oracle spanning routing, HTML/JSON/feeds, conditional-GET/ETag, rate-limit headers, byte-exact media, concurrency and shared-queue claim races — reflecting the grader's normalization faithfully, re-run continuously as a regression gate, plus checks for the hard constraints (no Ruby in process tree, 40 MB binary, /_health latency ratio).

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems match the reference vs. remain broken/unported across the long horizon, and detecting thrash.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With so many subsystems and shared state, it is easy to lose track of what already passed, regress a passing subsystem while fixing another, or loop on one endpoint; an accurate done-vs-remaining ledger sustains forward progress.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; declares done based on the last thing touched.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of what works; no guard against regressions when changing shared code.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of subsystem parity status and updates it as pieces pass.
anchors.8: Tracks per-subsystem pass/fail from the differential harness, notices when a change regresses a previously-passing area, and recognizes when stuck on one mismatch and reallocates attention.
anchors.10: Maintains a precise, harness-backed coverage ledger across all subsystems and constraints, distinguishes 'passing / failing / not-yet-attempted', catches circular re-debugging early and explicitly changes tactic, and uses coverage to prioritize the highest-value remaining parity gaps.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when a mismatch reveals a wrong assumption about reference behavior, a framework/crate limitation, or a constraint conflict — rather than forcing the current approach.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reverse-engineered contracts will be wrong in places; a chosen web framework or template engine may not reproduce a header set or Liquid rendering exactly; the agent must re-derive from the reference and sometimes swap approach instead of hard-coding around symptoms.

anchors.0: Ignores mismatches or papers over them with hacks that break other cases; barrels ahead on falsified assumptions.
anchors.3: Fixes individual mismatches locally but never questions the underlying assumption or design choice that caused a class of failures.
anchors.5: When a diff appears, returns to the reference to find the true behavior and corrects the implementation, including occasional small design changes.
anchors.8: Treats recurring mismatches as signals to revisit design (e.g. changing how headers/CSP are assembled, how ORM ordering/soft-delete is modeled, or how the job claim transaction is done) and re-verifies the whole affected subsystem after the change.
anchors.10: Diagnoses root causes across subsystems, makes decisive approach changes when a library or model can't reach parity (including under the no-Ruby/40 MB/latency constraints), updates the behavioral model and plan accordingly, and confirms the correction closed the class of failures without regressions.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring
dimensions.description: Continuously honoring the non-negotiable prohibitions/limits: no Ruby runtime or Ruby-bridge crates, no proxying/TCP to the reference, 40 MB release binary, latency parity, and exact shared-DB claim semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: These are pass/fail gates independent of feature parity; a design that quietly violates them (e.g. shelling to the reference to pass a hard subsystem, or a binary over 40 MB) can invalidate otherwise-correct work, so they must be tracked as first-class constraints throughout.

anchors.0: Ignores the constraints; risks proxying/embedding Ruby or blows the binary/latency budget without noticing.
anchors.3: Aware of the rules in the abstract but never checks them until (or unless) something breaks.
anchors.5: Keeps the constraints in mind and verifies the obvious ones once (no Ruby-bridge crates, binary size builds under cap).
anchors.8: Actively guards each constraint during development — audits Cargo.toml, checks process tree has no Ruby, monitors binary size and /_health latency ratio, and treats the shared-DB claim semantics as a matched contract.
anchors.10: Bakes constraint checks into the verification loop as standing gates (size, latency ratio, process-tree/no-TCP audit, BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter interop with the live reference), catching a violation the moment it is introduced rather than at the end.
